items.description: Person 2 describes the feedback process in Nepalese projects as 'pretty slow,' which hindered progress.
items.stochastic_link: This metaphor maps to **dynamic_forecast_adjustment** and **probabilistic_variance**. The delay and inconsistency in receiving client feedback introduce instability and uncertainty into project timelines and model refinement, forcing constant re-evaluation of goals (baseline erosion) similar to how probabilistic models require constant updates with new, uncertain data.
items.quote: 'the feedback loop was like pretty slow back in Nepal, so. We had to work for like a very long time to come up with like. A viable solution'

items.description: Person 2 describes Nepalese management as inflexible, requiring justification for personal time (e.g., holidays, sick leave) and being 'invasive to our personal life.'
items.stochastic_link: This maps to **data_dependency** and **opaque_outcomes**. The rigid, top-down control over information and process mirrors an over-reliance on a single, inflexible source of truth (historical management practice) without openness to new, emergent data (employee needs, context). This creates an opaque decision-making environment where outcomes (e.g., team morale, project pace) are hard to explain or optimize, akin to a model overly dependent on biased or incomplete historical data.
items.quote: 'they're a bit more invasive to our personal life... if you want like a holiday, you just shoot out a mail... they don't, you know, really care about. What you're doing?'

items.description: Person 2 discusses the difficulty of interpreting tone and intent in a new cultural context, unsure if colleagues are joking or being serious.
items.stochastic_link: This directly maps to **opaque_outcomes** and **non_deterministic_outputs**. Social and professional cues (inputs) do not produce consistent, interpretable responses (outputs). The same action (a joke) can have vastly different interpretations, creating a social environment of unpredictable and hard-to-explain interactions, paralleling the 'black box' nature of some complex models.
items.quote: 'I don't know from the tone whether if they're joking or not... for me, it's not. 100% sure... whether they're like joking or whether maybe I should joke along with them.'

items.description: Implied in Person 2's description of clients in Nepal who 'didn't necessarily know what they actually wanted' and lacked data-sharing standards.
items.stochastic_link: This maps to **lack_of_reproducibility** and **data_dependency**. Attempting to build a model (a solution) without clear, consistent requirements (a blueprint) or access to the necessary raw materials (data) makes it impossible to reliably produce the same result twice. The project's path becomes non-linear and highly dependent on the fluctuating clarity and cooperation of the client.
items.quote: 'it was really difficult to. Communicate the feedbacks, right? And it was like very difficult to get feedbacks as well... they had very less idea about... what they actually wanted.'

items.source_text: attribution to company size, not culture
items.description: Person 2 explicitly states that differences in project planning and process are due to company size (startup vs. established) rather than cultural background.
items.stochastic_implication: This contradicts the premise that cultural factors inherently introduce a form of **probabilistic_variance** or **non-linear estimation** into project management. He suggests process variability is deterministic and predictable based on organizational scale, not an irreducible uncertainty stemming from human cultural differences.
items.quote: 'I think it depends on. The type of the company, rather than the culture, I think.'

items.source_text: managerial impact as a technical problem
items.description: Person 2 identifies poor management (micromanagement) as a key hindrance to success but frames it as a universal trait of 'technical people' being 'wired to think' a certain way, not as a culturally-influenced friction point.
items.stochastic_implication: This downplays culture-specific **management_frictions** like **accountability_challenges** or **baseline_erosion**. He attributes the issue to a generic technical mindset, suggesting the problem and its solution are more about individual skills/awareness than navigating culturally-grounded, uncertain dynamics in authority and communication.
items.quote: 'a lot of people in tech, they don't have experience with management, right?... they tend to... focus more on micromanagement... I don't think it's got to do anything with. The culture background of the manager.'

items.description: Person 2 notes he is 'expected to behave in... American way' and does not expect his American colleagues to be 'sensitive towards my culture.' He has adapted unilaterally.
items.stochastic_implication: This perspective minimizes the mutual, interactive uncertainty (**dynamic_forecast_adjustment**) that cross-cultural teams introduce. It presents the cultural integration as a settled, one-sided adjustment rather than an ongoing, probabilistic negotiation where both sides' behaviors and expectations might need to co-evolve, creating inherent unpredictability in team dynamics.
items.quote: 'I'm expected to behave in in, like American way... I don't expect them to be. Sensitive towards my culture, right?'
